analysis.one_liner: Cuts red-tape delays for Medicare Advantage patients needing high-cost care and drugs.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 with one Republican cosponsor, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and has seen no hearings, votes, or floor action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directs the Health and Human Services Department to audit which Medicare Advantage prior-authorization rules cause the most paperwork for the most expensive items, services, and drugs [S2]. By May 2028, the agency must write one standard set of prior-authorization rules for those items across every Medicare Advantage plan, and it must waive the requirements altogether for care furnished by providers in risk-sharing groups like accountable care organizations [S2]. Prior authorization is the process where an insurer must sign off before a treatment or drug is covered, and delays in it are a leading complaint of Medicare Advantage patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans who face delays or denials when their doctor orders expensive imaging, procedures, or prescriptions, and the doctors who currently spend staff time filing repeated authorization paperwork. Providers in two-sided risk models would be freed from these requirements entirely for their patients [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage patients and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Requires a government audit, due by January 1, 2027, to identify the highest-reimbursement items and drugs where prior authorization demands excessive steps but clinical evidence would support a single standard policy [S2].

Requires a final rule by May 1, 2028 applying standardized prior-authorization requirements — including the same supplemental forms — to those items across all Medicare Advantage plans, so patients are not subject to a different gauntlet depending on their plan [S2].

Exempts care furnished by providers participating in two-sided risk models, such as accountable care organizations, from prior authorization for those items, on the theory that providers sharing financial risk already have an incentive to order care responsibly [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it passes, Medicare Advantage insurers would lose some of their ability to slow or deny the most expensive care, and the Medicare program and taxpayers could face somewhat higher costs if utilization rises once authorization barriers drop. The Health and Human Services Department would also bear the cost of the audit and rulemaking.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare Advantage insurers and the Medicare program

drawbacks.text: The relief is slow and narrow: the audit is due in 2027 and the standardized rules not until May 1, 2028, and they cover only items the Secretary identifies under the bill's three criteria, leaving most prior-authorization requirements untouched [S2].

Key standards are undefined — the bill requires the audit to flag items where prior authorization 'requires an excessive number of steps' without defining what excessive means, giving the agency wide discretion over how much actually changes [S2].

Removing authorization checks for high-reimbursement items, especially the blanket exemption for risk-bearing provider groups, could raise Medicare spending if it leads to more use of the costliest services and drugs, a cost ultimately shared by taxpayers and beneficiaries through premiums [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and well-documented burden on seniors and their doctors, and standardizing rules across plans could cut down arbitrary plan-by-plan variation. But the relief arrives late (2028), covers only a slice of prior-authorization decisions, leaves the key definition to agency discretion, and risks modestly higher Medicare spending. A designed-from-scratch fix could have moved faster and further.

outcome.mechanism: It sits in the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action — no hearing, no vote, no floor consideration — since the bill was referred there in February 2026.

narrative.text: Senator Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on February 3, 2026 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which holds jurisdiction over Medicare [S4].
It has one cosponsor, a Republican [S3].
No further action — no hearing, markup, or vote — has occurred since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, Medicare Advantage insurers keep their prior-authorization gatekeeping over the most expensive care unchanged, while seniors waiting on treatments get no relief. The bill is not yet dead, but it is moving nowhere.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the only partisan signal is one Democratic sponsor joined by one Republican cosponsor, suggesting at least nominal bipartisan interest.

industries.note: The bill would strip these insurers of plan-by-plan discretion to require prior authorization for the most expensive items and drugs, and forbid blanket waivers for providers in risk-sharing arrangements only with government sign-off. Prior-authorization gatekeeping is a core way MA plans manage costs and enrollment decisions, so standardized rules directly constrain their business model.

industries.industry: Accountable care organizations and other two-sided risk provider groups
industries.note: Care they furnish would be exempt from prior authorization for the covered items, making participation in risk-sharing models more attractive relative to traditional fee-for-service practice. Their incentive to order care appropriately is financial, which is why the bill ties the exemption to shared risk.

Standardized requirements and forms across all MA plans would cut the administrative burden of tracking dozens of different authorization protocols. That savings flows mostly to provider staff time rather than directly to patients.

analysis.trajectory: A newly referred bill with a single cosponsor and no committee action in its first months faces long odds; most bills at this stage die quietly in committee unless they gather many more cosponsors or get attached to a larger Medicare package moving through the Finance Committee.
